title: Stage 4: Update and delete
summary: Finish CRUD with PUT, DELETE and PATCH, and learn which requests are safe to repeat.

steps.title: Changing and removing
body: Tasks can be listed and created. A task tracker also needs to change them and throw them away. That completes **CRUD**: create, read, update, delete.
| Method | On a collection `/tasks` | On an item `/tasks/2` |
This stage adds the bottom three.
`PUT /tasks/2` means: *make task 2 look exactly like this body*. The client sends every field it is allowed to set, not just the one that changed:
The id comes from the URL. It is not in the body, because a client must not be able to renumber a task.
One handler, two sources: `id` is bound from the route because the route has an `{id}`, and the record is bound from the JSON body.

pairs: Create a new resource in a collection

steps.title: Idempotency
body: Networks fail in an awkward way: a client sends a request, the connection drops, and the client cannot tell whether the server acted on it. Should it send the request again?
That depends on whether the method is **idempotent**. An operation is idempotent when doing it twice leaves the server in the same state as doing it once.
- `PUT /tasks/2` with the same body, sent five times: task 2 ends up identical every time.
- `DELETE /tasks/2`, sent five times: task 2 is gone, and stays gone.
- `POST /tasks`, sent five times: five new tasks.

So a client may retry a GET, PUT or DELETE without thinking, and must be careful with a POST. This is a promise that *you*, the server author, keep. Nothing in the framework stops you from writing a PUT that appends, so do not.

Idempotent is about the **state on the server**, not about the response. The second `DELETE /tasks/2` answers `404` where the first answered `204`, and that is fine: the task is equally gone after both.

steps.prompt: A flaky connection makes a client send each request twice. Which are harmless to repeat?
buckets: Idempotent: same state as sending once
Not idempotent: the repeat changes more
steps.explain: A POST creates something new each time: two tasks, two payments. PUT and DELETE describe an end state ("it looks like this", "it is gone"), and repeating a description of the end state changes nothing more.

steps.prompt: Records are immutable, so an update swaps in a changed copy. What does this print?
code: tasks[index] = tasks[index] with { Title = "Build a REST API", Done = true };
record TaskItem(int Id, string Title, bool Done);
steps.explain: `with` makes a copy with some properties changed, and assigning it to `tasks[index]` replaces the old record in the same position, so the count stays 2. `FindIndex` returns `-1` when nothing matches: that is your 404.

steps.title: Replace a task
prompt: Add `PUT /tasks/{id}`, which replaces the title and done state of an existing task.
- Bind the body to a record `UpdateTask(string? Title, bool Done)`.
- No task with that id: `404 Not Found`.
- Invalid title (the same rules as `POST`: blank, or longer than 100 characters): `400 Bad Request` with `{"error":"..."}`, and the task is left unchanged.
- Otherwise store the new title and done value under the same id and respond `200 OK` with the updated task.
- The task keeps its id and its position in the list. `PUT` never adds a task.
Sending the same `PUT` twice must give the same result both times.
Everything from the earlier stages must keep working.

steps.title: DELETE and 204 No Content
body: `DELETE /tasks/2` removes task 2. After a successful delete there is nothing left to show, and HTTP has a status for exactly that: **`204 No Content`**. It means *done, and there is no body*.
`RemoveAll` returns how many items it removed, which tells you whether the note was there in the first place.
A `DELETE` request has no body either. Everything the server needs is in the URL.
You now have three success codes, and each says something different:
| `200 OK` | here is the result | yes |
| `201 Created` | a new resource exists, see `Location` | usually |
| `204 No Content` | it worked, nothing to send | never |

prompt: A client sends `DELETE /tasks/2` and gets `204`. The reply was slow, so the client's retry logic sends the same request again and gets `404`.
options: Yes. After one request or two, the server is in the same state: task 2 is gone.
No. An idempotent method must return the same status code every time.
No. The second request should have answered 204 as well, or the API is broken.
Only if the server remembers deleted ids and treats them specially.
steps.explain: Idempotency is about the effect on the server, not the response. The retry did no extra damage, which is what the client needed. Answering 404 the second time is the common choice, and an honest one: at that moment there is no task 2.

steps.title: Delete a task
prompt: - When the task exists: remove it and respond `204 No Content` with an empty body.
- When it does not: `404 Not Found`. That includes deleting the same task a second time.
After a delete, `GET /tasks/2` is `404` and `GET /tasks` no longer lists the task.
`GET`, `POST` and `PUT` must keep working. New ids still come from the highest id that exists: with tasks 1 and 3 left, the next task created gets id 4.

steps.title: PATCH: change one thing
body: Ticking a task off is the most common change of all. With `PUT`, the client must send the title too, even though it is not changing, and must first know what the title is.
**`PATCH`** is the method for a *partial* update: change what the body mentions, keep the rest.
One simple design gives the changeable part its own URL:
`/tasks/2/done` reads as *the done state of task 2*. The route has a fixed segment after the parameter:
The response is the whole updated resource, so the client can refresh what it shows without a second request.

steps.prompt: A phone app shows a checkbox next to each task. The user ticks one. The app knows the task's id but has not loaded its title. Which request fits best?
steps.explain: PATCH changes one part and leaves the rest. The PUT would replace the whole task with one that has no title, which your API rejects with 400. POST would try to create a task, and a GET must never change anything.
